S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.

subtypes.Contamination Obsessions: Recurrent and intrusive worries about contamination, germs, or dirt.
subtypes.Pathological Doubt: Pathological doubt regarding safety or mistakes, such as whether doors are locked or gas valves are closed.
subtypes.Symmetry and Exactness Obsessions: A strong urge that items must be lined up exactly or be symmetrical.
subtypes.Forbidden or Taboo Thoughts: Intrusive thoughts involving aggressive (harming others), sexual, or religious content that are prohibited.
subtypes.Somatic Obsessions: Persistent and specific fear that one might have a serious disease.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.

subtypes.Cleaning or Washing Compulsions: Repetitive acts to remove contamination, such as hand washing, showering, or excessive cleaning.
subtypes.Checking Compulsions: Repeatedly checking items like door locks, gas stoves, or switches to prevent danger.
subtypes.Ordering and Arranging Compulsions: Organizing objects in a specific order or at a precise angle to reduce anxiety.
subtypes.Mental Acts: Mental rituals performed internally, such as praying, counting, or repeating specific words silently.
subtypes.Repeating Rituals: Repeating specific actions (e.g., standing up, passing through a door) a set number of times.

symptom.disease_info: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by recurrent, intrusive thoughts, images, or urges (obsessions) and/or repetitive behaviors or mental acts (compulsions) that the person feels driven to perform, typically aimed at reducing distress or preventing feared events. The obsessions and compulsions are time-consuming or cause significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. Onset is often in late childhood to early adulthood, with a chronic, waxing-and-waning course that may be exacerbated by stress, role transitions, or medical events. OCD is distinguished from anxiety disorders and obsessive-compulsive personality traits by the presence of ego-dystonic, intrusive phenomena and ritualized responses, rather than simply excessive worry or rigid, but accepted, personality styles.

patient.personality: Candace is a structured, detail-oriented yet sociable operations leader who channels her perfectionism into organized projects, outdoor activities, and community engagement.
patient.stressor: Over the past several years, Candace’s role at the regional retail chain expanded, leaving her responsible for multiple underperforming stores, large staffing shortages, and a high-stakes digital transformation project with tight deadlines. Her long-standing tendency toward perfectionism and responsibility for people’s livelihoods made her increasingly preoccupied with the possibility of making a critical error—misreporting figures, missing safety issues, or overlooking compliance details that could harm the company or her team. As she started working later into the evenings and bringing work home mentally, she found it harder to “shut off,” and her usual coping outlets like hiking and yoga no longer fully relieved her mounting sense of internal pressure. When her preoccupation with potential mistakes began slowing down decisions at work, straining her relationships with colleagues and frustrating her spouse, she agreed to seek psychiatric care after realizing that her own thought patterns had become overwhelming and were interfering with her ability to lead effectively.
patient.chief_complaint: “I can’t get these unwanted thoughts about things going wrong at work out of my head, no matter how much I try to push them away.”

S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.
S065.manifestation: Lately my head just fills up with these images of spreadsheets with the wrong numbers, or a fire starting in one of the stores because I missed some tiny safety detail, and even when I’m at home trying to watch TV with my husband I keep mentally replaying worst-case scenarios and arguing with myself about whether I’ve forgotten something critical.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.
S066.manifestation: To calm myself down, I end up rereading the same emails and reports over and over, zooming in on tiny details, double- and triple-checking that I sent things correctly or that policies are followed, and I’ll sit there mentally going through each store one by one, almost like a silent checklist in my head, until it feels “just right” enough that I can move on to the next task.
